teaser: Matisse came home from Morocco envying men who could watch a fishbowl for hours.
review_notes:
Matisse in Tangier from late January to mid April 1912; painting made at Issy-les-Moulineaux in spring or early summer 1912.
Matisse buying the Issy house in 1912 (rented since 1909): check.
His remark about Moroccans contemplating goldfish bowls is reported in the literature; paraphrased, not quoted.
Setting usually described as the garden or conservatory at Issy.
Goldfish appearing in around nine or ten of his works: kept vague as “about ten”.
Pushkin Museum since 1948: check.

lesson.text: By 1912 Henri Matisse was forty-two and, for the first time, comfortable. A Russian collector bought his large canvases almost as fast as he could paint them. That year he was able to buy the house outside Paris that he had been renting, with its garden, its greenhouse and a studio among the trees.

Comfortable, but worn out. Paris critics still mocked him, and younger painters were turning to Cubism. In January he sailed to Tangier, in Morocco, hoping for light. It rained for weeks. When the sun came back he stayed until April and painted gardens, doorways and people sitting still.

What struck him most in Tangier was a habit. He noticed that local men could spend hours daydreaming over a goldfish bowl, doing nothing else at all. To a Frenchman who could not stop working, this looked like wisdom.

Back home that spring, he set a glass cylinder with four goldfish on a garden table and painted it, on a canvas nearly 1.5 meters tall (about 4 feet 9 inches). The fish are the smallest things in it. So why can't you look anywhere else?

lesson.title: Why the fish win
lesson.text: Three reasons, all of them about color.

spots.title: Orange on green
spots.text: Pure orange-red, set in pale green water and ringed by green leaves. Orange and green sit far apart on the color wheel, so each makes the other vibrate.

spots.title: Seen twice
spots.text: Higher up, four loose orange smears: the same fish as they appear through the surface of the water. No eyes, no fins, only color drifting.

spots.title: The dark surround
spots.text: Blue-black fills the gaps on the right. Against it the bowl seems lit from inside, like a lamp.

lesson.text: Those smears on the surface tell you something odd about where you are standing. You see the fish from the side, through the glass, and at the same moment from above, through the water. A camera could not do both. Matisse can, and he does it with the furniture too.
Compare the shape of the table with the shape of the bowl standing on it.

lines.label: The tabletop
lines.text: A round table seen from the side would be a thin oval. This one is nearly a full circle, as if you were hovering above it.

lines.label: The glass wall
lines.text: Yet the side of the bowl is a straight vertical. For this you must be standing in front of it, at eye level.

lines.label: One leg
lines.text: A single turquoise leg holds the tilted table up. Nothing slides off, because the whole picture has agreed to be flat.

lesson.text: Matisse combines several viewpoints so you get the most complete idea of each thing: the roundness of the table, the height of the bowl, the fish from the side and from above.

He had learned part of this from Paul Cézanne, whose tilted tabletops he admired, and part from the carpets and tiles he had studied in Morocco and at a great exhibition of Islamic art in Munich in 1910. In those objects, pattern runs evenly from edge to edge and nothing is pushed into the background.

The paint is thinner than it looks in reproduction. Around many leaves and along the edge of the table Matisse left slivers of bare, cream-colored canvas instead of drawing outlines. Those unpainted threads are what make the colors seem to breathe.

spots.title: A staring eye
spots.text: One fish faces you head on, two black dots for eyes. It is a small comic touch in a very composed picture.

spots.title: Pink behind green
spots.text: At the top the background turns candy pink, dotted with round green leaves. It reads as wall, wallpaper and garden all at once.

spots.title: Purple flowers
spots.text: Violet blooms nod on thin stems. Purple is the one color here that belongs to neither the fish nor the foliage, and it cools the top right corner.

spots.title: The garden seat
spots.text: The curved turquoise arm of a bench or chair sweeps up the left edge, striped with quick dark and light strokes.

spots.title: Ground level
spots.text: Pink flowers and clumps of leaves float on darkness at the bottom right. Matisse does not say whether they are in pots or in the ground.

spots.title: Yellow leaves
spots.text: A small plant in an orange pot stands on the table. Its yellow-green leaves repeat the fish colors in a quieter voice.

lesson.text: Goldfish swim through about ten of his pictures over the next few years. They became his private sign for a state of mind: calm attention, with nothing to achieve. He had once written that he wanted his art to soothe a tired mind. The fishbowl was that idea given a body.

The collector Sergei Shchukin bought this canvas and took it to Moscow, where it has stayed. It now hangs in the Pushkin Museum. And the four fish go on doing the one thing Matisse traveled to Africa to learn: circling slowly, in no hurry, watched by someone with time.

quiz.question: Where had Matisse just been when he painted Goldfish in 1912?
quiz.explanation: He spent the first months of 1912 in Tangier.

quiz.question: What habit of people in Tangier impressed him?
options: Daydreaming for hours over a goldfish bowl
quiz.explanation: He admired how they could contemplate a fishbowl for hours.

quiz.question: Why do the orange fish stand out so strongly?
options: They are painted larger than life
They are surrounded by green, a contrasting color
quiz.explanation: Orange and green sit far apart on the color wheel and strengthen each other.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the table?
options: It is seen from above while the bowl is seen from the side
quiz.explanation: The tabletop is nearly a full circle, but the glass wall is a straight vertical.

quiz.question: What are the orange smears near the top of the bowl?
options: The fish seen through the water's surface
quiz.explanation: They show the same four fish from above.

facts.text: In 1912 Matisse was poor and could not sell his paintings.
facts.explanation: A Russian collector was buying his large canvases, and he was able to buy his house that year.

facts.text: Matisse left thin strips of bare canvas between some shapes instead of drawing outlines.
facts.explanation: Slivers of unpainted canvas separate leaves and edges.

facts.text: Goldfish appear in only this one painting by Matisse.
facts.explanation: They return in about ten of his works.
